Modified large-NN approach to gapless spin liquids, magnetic orders, and dynamics: Application to triangular lattice antiferromagnets

Anjishnu Bose Email: anjishnu.bose@mail.utoronto.ca Affiliation: Department of Physics, University of Toronto, 60 St. George Street, Toronto, ON, M5S 1A7 Canada    Kathleen Hart Affiliation: Department of Physics, University of Toronto, 60 St. George Street, Toronto, ON, M5S 1A7 Canada    Ruairidh Sutcliffe Affiliation: Department of Physics, University of Toronto, 60 St. George Street, Toronto, ON, M5S 1A7 Canada    Arun Paramekanti Email: arun.paramekanti@utoronto.ca Affiliation: Department of Physics, University of Toronto, 60 St. George Street, Toronto, ON, M5S 1A7 Canada
August 24, 2026
Abstract

Recent work has shown that the triangular lattice spin-1/21/2 J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} Heisenberg and XXZ antiferromagnets may exhibit coplanar or supersolid orders proximate to a gapless Dirac spin liquid phase. We explore a distinct S​U​(2​N)×S​U​(M)SU(2N)\!\!\times\!\!SU(M) fermionic parton approach, complemented by variational Monte Carlo calculations for the spin-1/21/2 model, to study the phase diagram of these models. We also calculate their dynamical spin response including parton interactions within a random phase approximation, and discuss implications for neutron scattering on triangular lattice cobaltates Ba3CoSb2O9, Na2BaCo(PO4)2, K2Co(SeO3)2, Rb2Co(SeO3)2, and Yb-based magnet KYbSe2.

I Introduction

Understanding the quantum spin dynamics of strongly frustrated spin-1/21/2 systems remains an important problem in magnetism. While sharp magnon modes in an ordered magnet are correctly described by linear spin-wave theory (LSWT) [1, 2], incorporating magnon interactions to go beyond LSWT [3, 4, 5] is necessary to capture quantitative renormalizations of the spin wave dispersion as well as the possible breakdown of magnons [6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12]. LSWT and the leading corrections to LWST may be formally justified within a 1/S1/S expansion for large spin-SS. However, for spin-1/21/2 systems, series expansion techniques have shown that there are interesting features in the spin dynamics which seem beyond the purview of an interacting magnon approach, including unusual roton-like features in the excitation spectrum [13, 14]. The discoveries of several highly frustrated spin-1/21/2 magnetic materials which defy ordering down to temperatures well below the Curie-Weiss scale, i.e. with TN≪θCWT_{N}\ll\theta_{\rm CW}, also suggests that an alternative framework to describe their quantum spin dynamics, perhaps in terms of fractionalized parton degrees of freedom, might provide a useful perspective.

A well-studied route to fractionalization is to express spin-1/21/2 degrees of freedom in terms of constrained Schwinger bosons via

𝐒=12​bα†​𝝈α​β​bβ;bα†​bα=1\mathbf{S}=\frac{1}{2}b^{\dagger}_{\alpha}\bm{\sigma}_{\alpha\beta}b^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\beta};~~b^{\dagger}_{\alpha}b^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\alpha}=1\, (1)

with implicit sum on spinor indices. Generalizing this formulation to α=1​…​N\alpha=1\ldots N and replacing 𝝈α​β\bm{\sigma}_{\alpha\beta} by S​U​(N)SU(N) generators leads to the S​U​(N)SU(N) Schwinger boson formulation which allows one to describe both the ordered collinear Néel antiferromagnet on the square lattice as well as gapped dimerized magnets in Heisenberg models within a large-NN framework [15, 16, 17, 18], separated by an unconventional quantum critical point involving partons coupled to fluctuating U⁡(1)U(1) gauge fields [19]. A distinct S​p​(2​N)Sp(2N) generalization involves generalizing two-component bosons to NN flavors of two-component bosons (with an additional flavor index ℓ=1​…​N\ell=1\ldots N) [20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26]. The spin rotation invariant Hamiltonian is then generalized as (with implicit sums on flavor and spinor indices)

H\displaystyle H =\displaystyle= J​∑⟨i,j⟩ϵα​β​bi​ℓ​α†​bj​ℓ​β†​ϵμ​ν​bi​ℓ′​μ​bj​ℓ′​ν\displaystyle J\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle}\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}b^{\dagger}_{i\ell\alpha}b^{\dagger}_{j\ell\beta}\epsilon_{\mu\nu}b^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i\ell^{\prime}\mu}b^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{j\ell^{\prime}\nu} (2)

with the constraint bi​ℓ​α†​bi​ℓ​α=2​N​κb^{\dagger}_{i\ell\alpha}b^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i\ell\alpha}=2N\kappa at each site ii. The physical limit of the spin model corresponds to N=1N=1 and κ=1/2\kappa=1/2, but more generally the filling factor κ\kappa plays the role of a ‘spin’. This formulation is useful to describe geometrically frustrated magnets at large NN, with gapped singlet ℤ2{\mathbb{Z}}_{2} spin liquids appearing at small spin κ<κc\kappa<\kappa_{c} and non-collinear magnetically ordered phases appearing beyond a critical spin value κ>κc\kappa>\kappa_{c}.

In order to describe gapless spin liquid phases on the other hand, it is expedient to use a Schwinger fermion formulation [27, 28, 29, 30, 31]

𝐒=12​fα†​𝝈α​β​fβ;fα†​fα=1\mathbf{S}=\frac{1}{2}f^{\dagger}_{\alpha}\bm{\sigma}_{\alpha\beta}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\beta};~~f^{\dagger}_{\alpha}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\alpha}=1 (3)

The S​U​(N)SU(N) Schwinger boson approach naturally generalizes to Schwinger fermions, allowing one to describe gapless spin liquids at large NN [32, 33, 34, 35]. However, this does not allow for magnetic order in the leading large NN mean field limit. With decreasing NN, magnetic order can instead emerge from strong gauge field fluctuations necessitated by the local constraint, either via proliferation of monopoles which carry nontrivial spin quantum numbers [36, 37], or through four-fermion interaction terms which become relevant as NN is decreased, which fosters chiral symmetry breaking [33]. It is a challenge to study these competing effects in a controlled manner.

Motivated by this, we explore here a fermionic S​U​(2​N)×S​U​(M)SU(2N)\times SU(M) approach which allows one to study magnetically ordered states and gapless spin liquids on equal footing. For fixed κ=M/2​N\kappa=M/2N, and for N→∞N\to\infty this problem reduces to a magnetic order parameter Yukawa-coupled to fermions, reminiscent of other large-NN approaches to fermionic quantum critical points [38, 39, 40, 41], while decreasing NN leads to important gauge fluctuation corrections. We thus believe this approach might allow one to study fermionic quantum critical points and to systematically incorporate the impact of gauge fluctuations to study the spin liquid to magnetic ordering transition. We use this parton approach to obtain the mean field theory of the triangular antiferromagnet, which shows 120-degree coplanar order at large ‘spin’ and a Dirac spin liquid at small ‘spin’. Appendix A and B present further details of the parton theory, and its path integral formulation.

We then discuss a phenomenological extension of this approach to XXZ models which break the Heisenberg symmetry, and show that it can reasonably capture the ground state phase diagram of models which have been explored using density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) computations [42, 43, 44, 45]. We complement this with variational Monte Carlo (VMC) simulations of Gutzwiller projected Dirac wavefunctions with long range Jastrow factors which lead to results in good quantitative agreement with the DMRG results, and extending previous VMC results on the Heisenberg model [46, 47]. Details of the VMC are in Appendix C.

Finally, we turn to the study of the dynamical spin response of these models within the parton approach going beyond mean field theory to include parton interactions within a random phase approximation which captures recent neutron scattering results showing magnons coexisting with continuum scattering in pseudospin-1/21/2 triangular cobaltate magnets Ba3CoSb2O9  [48, 49, 50, 51], Na2BaCo(PO4)2 [52, 53, 54], K2Co(SeO3)2 [55, 56] and Rb2Co(SeO3)2 [57] and Yb-based magnets such as KYbSe2 [58].

Our semi-analytical approach is argued to provide insights into results obtained by more numerically intensive many-body methods such as density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) [59, 60], variational Monte Carlo (VMC) [61, 62], or pseudo-fermion functional renormalization group (pfFRG) [63, 64, 65] techniques which are used to study the ground states and spin excitations of diverse frustrated magnets.

II Parton theory

II.1 Heisenberg models

We begin by exploring a formal limit for Heisenberg models which describes the competition between disordered gapless spin-liquids and ordered symmetry-broken states for which mean-field theory is exact, a scenario which is sketched in Fig. 1. In such a limit, we expect that both spin liquid states and ordered states are energetically competitive, but all gauge fluctuations have been suppressed. Our work is inspired by the S​p​(2​N)Sp(2N) and large-S approaches [20, 66] to antiferromagnets. Using fermionic partons, we introduce a flavor index ℓ\ell in the fundamental representation of S​U​(M)SU(M), along with enlarging the physical internal symmetry group to S​U​(2​N)SU(2N). For partons at half-filling, assuming implicit summation on spinor and flavor indices, fi,α,ℓ†​fi,α,ℓ=N​Mf^{\dagger}_{i,\alpha,\ell}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i,\alpha,\ell}\!=\!NM at each site ii. The case of spin-1/21/2 in S​U​(2)SU(2) corresponds to N=1N\!=\!1 and M=1M\!=\!1. Now consider a Hamiltonian on bond (i,j)(i,j)

ℋi​j\displaystyle{\mathcal{H}}_{ij} =\displaystyle= 𝕁i​j​fi,α,ℓ†​Tα​βa​fi,β,ℓ​fj,μ,ℓ′†​Tμ​νa​fj,ν,ℓ′\displaystyle{\mathbb{J}}_{ij}f^{\dagger}_{i,\alpha,\ell}T^{a}_{\alpha\beta}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i,\beta,\ell}f^{\dagger}_{j,\mu,\ell^{\prime}}T^{a}_{\mu\nu}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{j,\nu,\ell^{\prime}} (4)

where TaT^{a} are the 4​N2−14N^{2}-1 generators of S​U​(2​N)SU(2N) in the fundamental representation. Using the completeness relation of the generators, we can rewrite this in the form

ℋi​j\displaystyle{\mathcal{H}}_{ij} =\displaystyle= 12​𝕁i​j​fi,α,ℓ†​fi,β,ℓ​fj,β,ℓ′†​fj,α,ℓ′+const.\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}{\mathbb{J}}_{ij}f^{\dagger}_{i,\alpha,\ell}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i,\beta,\ell}f^{\dagger}_{j,\beta,\ell^{\prime}}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{j,\alpha,\ell^{\prime}}+\mathrm{const.} (5)

In the quantum spin liquid, ⟨fi,α,ℓ†​fj,β,ℓ′⟩=δα​β​δℓ,ℓ′​χi​j\langle f^{\dagger}_{i,\alpha,\ell}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{j,\beta,\ell^{\prime}}\rangle\!=\!\delta_{\alpha\beta}\delta_{\ell,\ell^{\prime}}\chi_{ij} with χi​j∼𝒪⁡(1)\chi_{ij}\!\sim\!{\mathcal{O}}(1). By contrast, deep in a magnetically ordered state, it suffices to consider single-site order with ⟨fi,α,ℓ†​fj,β,ℓ′⟩∼δi​j​δℓ,ℓ′​N​mia​Tα​βa\langle f^{\dagger}_{i,\alpha,\ell}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{j,\beta,\ell^{\prime}}\rangle\!\sim\!\delta_{ij}\delta_{\ell,\ell^{\prime}}\sqrt{N}m_{i}^{a}T^{a}_{\alpha\beta}, with mia​mia∼𝒪⁡(1)m^{a}_{i}m^{a}_{i}\sim{\mathcal{O}}(1). Magnetic ordering corresponds to splitting the 2​N2N levels into two sets of NN levels and occupying the lower NN levels, which amounts to switching on Weiss fields which couple to NN generators out of a total of 4​N2−14N^{2}-1 generators. These NN Weiss fields can be viewed as NN copies of a conventional S​U​(2)SU(2) Weiss field, each of which Zeeman splits one pair of the 2N levels. The resulting Hartree-Fock mean-field expectation value of the Hamiltonian thus scales as ⟨ℋi​j⟩mf∼𝕁i​j​(−N2​M​|χi​j|2+N​M2​𝐦i⋅𝐦j)\langle{\mathcal{H}}_{ij}\rangle_{\rm mf}\sim{\mathbb{J}}_{ij}(-N^{2}M|\chi_{ij}|^{2}+NM^{2}\mathbf{m}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{m}_{j}). Scaling the exchange coupling as 𝕁i​j=J/N{\mathbb{J}}_{ij}=J/N yields ⟨ℋi​j⟩mf∼Ji​j​(−N​M​|χi​j|2+M2​𝐦i⋅𝐦j)\langle{\mathcal{H}}_{ij}\rangle_{\rm mf}\sim J_{ij}(-NM|\chi_{ij}|^{2}+M^{2}\mathbf{m}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{m}_{j}).  This mean field result, in the  usual manner, is expected to become exact in the limit of large M,N→∞M,N\to\infty with fixed κ=M/2​N\kappa=M/2N. The ratio κ\kappa plays the role of ‘spin’ in a manner similar to the S​p​(2​N)Sp(2N) framework. We can construct the appropriately defined local moment sum-rule in this large-(N,M)(N,M) limit which yields κ⁡(κ+1)\kappa(\kappa+1); see Appendix A.

Finally, we briefly comment on the impact of fluctuations beyond mean field theory. In the usual S​U​(2​N)SU(2N) extension of fermionic theories sub-leading corrections to the spin susceptibility from gauge fluctuations appear as 𝒪⁡(1N){\cal O}(\frac{1}{N}) corrections [33, 34]. In our extension, since there again is a single local constraint, the gauge field will couple to all the N​MNM degrees of freedom, and we thus expect gauge fluctuation corrections to spin correlations to be more strongly suppressed as 𝒪⁡(1N​M){\cal O}(\frac{1}{NM}) or equivalently 𝒪⁡(1κ​N2){\cal O}(\frac{1}{\kappa N^{2}}). The spin response will however also get contributions from order parameter fluctuations - the leading order corrections will come from bubble diagrams within a random phase approximation which will contribute at 𝒪⁡(1N){\cal O}(\frac{1}{N}), and hence will be more important than gauge fluctuation corrections for M≫1M\gg 1; see Appendix A. In Fig. 1, we summarize this scenario for competing spin liquid and magnetically ordered phases.

II.2 Phenomenological mean field theory of Heisenberg models

From the above formulation of the spin model, we see that the effect of κ=M/2​N\kappa=M/2N is to reweight the energy contribution of the quantum spin liquid relative to magnetically ordered broken symmetry ground states. This reweighting factor can be recast phenomenologically by splitting the Hamiltonian ℋi​j{\mathcal{H}}_{ij} as a sum of two terms,

ℋi​j=α​ℋi​j+(1−α)​ℋi​j,{\mathcal{H}}_{ij}=\alpha{\mathcal{H}}_{ij}+(1-\alpha){\mathcal{H}}_{ij}, (6)

and doing a mean field theory where we decouple the first term in a parton hopping channel (favoring a spin-liquid state), and the second term in a magnetic ordering channel assuming a local Weiss field (favoring a symmetry broken state). From the previous subsection, we can identify the ratio α/(1−α)≡N/M\alpha/(1-\alpha)\!\equiv\!N/M, so that α=N/(N+M)=1/(1+2​κ)\alpha\!=\!N/(N+M)\!=\!1/(1+2\kappa). Taking κ→∞\kappa\!\to\!\infty corresponds to α=0\alpha\!=\!0 which leads to a classical mean field treatment of the spin model, while the limit κ→0\kappa\!\to\!0 leads to α=1\alpha\!=\!1 which is the pure spin liquid limit. The physical model in this picture κ=1/2\kappa\!=\!1/2 corresponds to α=1/2\alpha\!=\!1/2. We can however explore tuning α\alpha (equivalently OPENκ)\kappa) as a way to explore both magnetically ordered and spin liquid phases and the quantum phase transition between them.

II.3 Phenomenological mean field theory of anisotropic spin-exchange models

If the spin-1/21/2 Hamiltonian has anisotropies which break the S​U​(2)SU(2) spin-rotation symmetry, there is no obvious large-(N,M)(N,M) extension. Nevertheless, motivated by the Heisenberg limit, one can still extend the phenomenological mean-field treatment from the previous subsection to such anisotropic models. We modify Eq.(6) to have symmetry-distinct parameters corresponding to different generators, and as well as incorporating possibly bond-dependence (e.g., first-neighbor versus second-neighbor). In other words, an anisotropic spin Hamiltonian on a bond ℋi​j{\mathcal{H}}_{ij} should be decomposed into a hopping channel (favoring a spin-liquid state), and a Weiss channel (favoring an ordered state), with some relative ratio of αi​ja:(1−αi​ja)\alpha_{ij}^{a}:(1-\alpha_{ij}^{a}) respectively. One can constrain the parameters in such an approach, i.e. fix the bond and component dependent parameters αi​ja\alpha^{a}_{ij}, using ground state properties like the phase boundaries from other numerical methods, or known order parameters. Once fixed, we can use these parameters to explore excitations via the RPA corrected spin response function which can be compared with spin dynamics observed in neutron scattering or resonant inelastic X-ray scattering experiments.

III Triangular lattice antiferromagnets

In the following sections, we will use the methodology introduced in Sec.II and apply it to a specific spin model. Namely, we look at a J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} XXZ spin model on the triangular lattice which consists of anti-ferromagnetic easy-axis interaction between nearest-neighbor and second-nearest-neighbour spins. The Hamiltonian on a bond has the form

ℋi​j=(Six​Sjx+Siy​Sjy+Δ​Siz​Sjz),{\mathcal{H}}_{ij}=\left(S_{i}^{x}S_{j}^{x}+S_{i}^{y}S_{j}^{y}+\Delta S_{i}^{z}S_{j}^{z}\right)\,, (7)

where Δ≥1\Delta\geq 1 represents the easy-axis anisotropy. The full Hamiltonian looks like

ℋ=J1​∑⟨i,j⟩1ℋi​j+J2​∑⟨i,j⟩2ℋi​j,J1,J2>0.{\mathcal{H}}=J_{1}\sum_{\expectationvalue{i, j}_{1}}{\mathcal{H}}_{ij}+J_{2}\sum_{\expectationvalue{i,j}_{2}}{\mathcal{H}}_{ij}\,,\>\>\>J_{1},J_{2}>0\,. (8)

where ⟨i,j⟩1\expectationvalue{i, j}_{1} and ⟨i,j⟩2\expectationvalue{i, j}_{2} is a shorthand for first-nearest and second-nearest neighbors on the triangular lattice. We will explore the impact of varying the anisotropy Δ\Delta away from its Heisenberg point Δ=1\Delta\!=\!1, and the strength of the second neighbor exchange which can frustrate conventional 120120-degree magnetic order of the Heisenberg model.

III.1 Spinon mean field ground state

In this section, we analyze the spin Hamiltonian in Eq.(8) at the mean-field level. We first study the Hamiltonian in the Heisenberg limit Δ=1\Delta=1 using our large-(N,M)(N,M) formalism and later modify the approach for the anisotropic case Δ>1\Delta>1.

III.1.1 Heisenberg Limit Δ=1\Delta=1

We consider a Hamiltonian of the form given in Eq.(4) on nearest and second-nearest neighbors on the triangular lattice in the N,M≫1N,M\gg 1 limit, extending the Heisenberg model. We get a phase diagram tuning the spin κ=M/2​N\kappa=M/2N, and exchange ratios J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1}. The self-consistent mean-field parameters we allow for in this analysis correspond to a S​U​(2​N)×S​U​(M)SU(2N)\times SU(M) symmetric hoppings for the spinons fi,α,ℓf_{i,\alpha,\ell} as ti​jα​β;ℓ​ℓ′=ti​j​δα​β​δℓ​ℓ′t_{ij}^{\alpha\beta;\ell\ell^{\prime}}=t_{ij}\delta^{\alpha\beta}\delta_{\ell\ell^{\prime}}. We also allow for local Weiss fields corresponding to a S​U​(2​N)SU(2N) generalization of magnetic orders for each flavor ℓ\ell. Any conventional S​U​(2)SU(2) order can be generalized to S​U​(2​N)×S​U​(M)SU(2N)\times SU(M) by simply having NN copies of the S​U​(2)SU(2) Weiss fields per flavor ℓ\ell in S​U​(M)SU(M). In principle one can expect more complicated orderings similar to multi-polar ordered state in the S​U​(2​N)SU(2N) limit. However, for simple Hamiltonians which exhibit collinear and coplanar orderings, any S​U​(2​N)SU(2N) extensions deep in the ordered phase can be shown to not have lower energies than just NN copies of the S​U​(2)SU(2) order, and hence we can restrict our Weiss fields for simplicity. The resultant phase diagram is shown in Fig.2.

We find that the ground state for κ≲0.3\kappa\lesssim 0.3 is the generalization of the symmetric π\pi-flux state on the triangular lattice which exhibits two Dirac nodes nested by wave-vectors 𝐐=𝐌1/2/3{{\bf{Q}}}={{\bf{M}}}_{1/2/3} in the Brillouin zone. This state does not break any internal and lattice symmetries. At the mean-field level, the second neighbor exchange interaction does not self-consistently generate any hoppings which may gap out the Dirac nodes. The nearest-neighbor hoppings in this Dirac spin liquid (DSL) can be determined self-consistently in terms of the exchange interactions and the strength is found to be |t1|≈0.2​N​J1|t_{1}|\approx 0.2NJ_{1}; see Appendix.D. We also find a range of spin κ≈0.35−0.37\kappa\approx 0.35-0.37 where the phase boundaries match qualitatively with many-body results from DMRG [42, 43, 45] and VMC [46, 47].

Then we study the order parameters generated at an “effective spin” of κ≈0.36\kappa\approx 0.36 and plot the results in Fig.3. At J2/J1=0J_{2}/J_{1}=0, we find an ordered moment of roughly ⟨S⟩≈0.35\expectationvalue{S}\approx 0.35 (out of a maximum of 0.50.5), which is in good qualitative agreement with previous results on the nearest-neighbor Heisenberg model on the triangular lattice using a variety of methods. Spin-wave corrections [67] and series expansions [68] find ⟨S⟩≈0.2−0.3\expectationvalue{S}\approx 0.2-0.3, while ED [69, 70], VMC [71], and DMRG [42, 43, 45] find ⟨S⟩≈0.3\langle S\rangle\approx 0.3-0.40.4. The effective spin being κ≈0.36\kappa\approx 0.36 is equivalent to the phenomenological parameter α≈0.6\alpha\approx 0.6. We also note that the order parameter will be further reduced due to spin-wave fluctuations.

III.1.2 Easy-axis anisotropy Δ>1\Delta>1

Now we introduce an easy-axis anisotropy in the Hamiltonian with Δ>1\Delta>1. As mentioned in Sec.II, we now have to introduce a phenomenological parameters αi​j\alpha_{ij} which have bond-dependence. Moreover, since the S​U​(2)SU(2) symmetry is broken, generically one can have αi​j⟂≠αi​jz\alpha_{ij}^{\perp}\neq\alpha_{ij}^{z}. For small anisotropies, one can split the full Hamiltonian into a Heisenberg part, and a small deviation from it. Subsequently, the Heisenberg part can be treated similar to the S​U​(2​N)×S​U​(M)SU(2N)\times SU(M) formalism with a fixed uniform α≈0.6\alpha\approx 0.6 as seen in the previous section. The deviation however needs an independent tuning parameter δ​αi​j\delta\alpha_{ij}.

Let us focus on just the nearest neighbor part of the Hamiltonian at a small anisotropy Δ\Delta. As mentioned above, one needs two parameters α1⟂\alpha_{1}^{\perp} and α1z\alpha_{1}^{z} which, for small anisotropies, can be recast as α1⟂=α−(Δ−1)​δ​α\alpha_{1}^{\perp}=\alpha-(\Delta-1)\delta\alpha and α1z=α+(Δ−1)​δ​α\alpha_{1}^{z}=\alpha+(\Delta-1)\delta\alpha. The classical order that we expect is the so-called Y-state which has a three sublattice magnetic unit-cell and consists of both in-plane and out-of plane spin components. This Y-state is also sometimes called a supersolid state in the language of hardcore bosons [72, 73, 74, 75, 76]. The out-of-plane spin component of the ordering is like a boson density solid, whereas the in-plane spin component corresponds to the phase of the boson in a superfluid state. In Fig.4, we plot how the three independent order parameter of a supersolid order develop as we tune δ​α\delta\alpha with a fixed α≈0.6\alpha\approx 0.6 as motivated from the effective spin κ≈0.36\kappa\approx 0.36 in the Heisenberg limit. We find that all three order parameters lie in the experimentally observed regime [52, 54] for δ​α≈0.1−0.15\delta\alpha\approx 0.1-0.15. Furthermore, the effective parton interaction in the phenomenological Hamiltonian Eq.(6) is in good agreement with [54] where they study a similar approach of residual interactions generating Weiss fields in the Dirac state.

III.2 Gutzwiller projected wavefunction

Going beyond mean field theory, we also studied the phase diagram of the J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} XXZ model using Gutzwiller projected parton wave-functions. We compute the energy and correlations of the projected wave-function through a Monte Carlo sampling of real space configurations which obey the strict Hilbert space constraint (that the fermionic spinons are at half-filling on each site). There has been previous variational numerics on the easy-axis nearest-neighbour XXZ model [71], as well as the Heisenberg limit of the J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} model on the triangular lattice [46, 47]. In this paper, we extend those numerics by looking at the easy-axis limit of the J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} XXZ model on the triangular lattice.

From the mean-field theory, we expect to find a supersolid order at small J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1}, a stripe order at large J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1} with possibly an intermediate spin liquid phase. Keeping that in mind, the variational parameters we allow for in our analysis are independent Weiss fields which can accommodate both the supersolid order and the stripe order, parton hoppings in the π\pi-flux state, as well as long-range isotropic Jastrow factors ; see Appendix C.

The results of the optimum energies in the DSL state, as well as DSL+order ansatzes are shown in Fig.5 and Fig.6. For a fixed J2/J1=0J_{2}/J_{1}=0, we find the ground state to be the coplanar 120∘120^{\circ} ordered state when the anisotropy is easy-plane, 0.5≤Δ<10.5\leq\Delta<1. Meanwhile, when the anisotropy is easy-axis, 1<Δ≤21<\Delta\leq 2, we find the ground state to be the Y-state, with the energetics consistent with previous VMC work [71]. Throughout, the pure DSL is closeby energetically and for that reason we posit that it can be treated as a parent spin liquid state for these symmetry broken phases [34]. Next, for a fixed anisotropy of Δ=1.5\Delta=1.5, we find the supersolid Y-state gives way to the pure DSL as the true ground state at small J2/J1≈0.03−0.04J_{2}/J_{1}\approx 0.03-0.04. As J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1} is increased, eventually the pure DSL transitions into the out-of-plane z-stripe order at J2/J1≈0.16−0.17J_{2}/J_{1}\approx 0.16-0.17. These are in good agreement with recent DMRG results[45].

IV Spin dynamics

In this section, we report the spin dynamics of the mean-field states after incorporating RPA corrections coming from magnon like excitations of the internal Weiss fields. First, we calculate the sublattice-resolved bare mean-field spin susceptibility of the spinons [77, 78, 79, 80, 81] using a simple bubble diagram

χ0,i​ja​b(𝐐,iΩ)=−∑𝐤,i​ωTr[σa2𝒢i​jT(𝐤,iω)σb2𝒢j​iT(𝐤+𝐐,iω+iΩ)],\chi_{0,ij}^{ab}({{\bf{Q}}},i\Omega)\!=\!-\!\!\sum_{{{\bf{k}}},\;i\omega}\!\!\text{Tr}[\frac{\sigma^{a}}{2}{\mathcal{G}}_{ij}^{T}({{\bf{k}}},i\omega)\frac{\sigma^{b}}{2}{\mathcal{G}}_{ji}^{T}({{\bf{k}}}+{{\bf{Q}}},i\omega+i\Omega)]\,, (9)

where a,ba\,,b represent spin-directions, and i,ji\,,j mark sublattices, and 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} is the bare spinon Green’s function. We note that this bare mean-field susceptibility can be calculated in both the symmetric DSL state, as well as broken symmetry DSL+ordering state. Following this, we can analytically continue Eq.(9) into real-frequency as χ0,i​ja​b​(𝐐,Ω+i​η)\chi_{0,ij}^{ab}({{\bf{Q}}},\Omega+i\eta). Incorporating RPA corrections to the response, we get

χi​ja​b(𝐐,Ω)=[(−𝒥(𝐐)⋅χ0(𝐐,Ω))−1⋅χ0(𝐐,Ω)]i​ja​b,\!\!\chi_{ij}^{ab}({{\bf{Q}}},\Omega)\!=\!\left[(\mathds{1}\!-\!{\mathcal{J}}({{\bf{Q}}})\!\cdot\!\chi_{0}({{\bf{Q}}},\Omega))^{-1}\!\cdot\!\chi_{0}({{\bf{Q}}},\Omega)\right]_{ij}^{ab}\,, (10)

where all algebraic operations like 𝒥⋅χ0{\mathcal{J}}\cdot\chi_{0}, or χ0−1\chi_{0}^{-1}, are shorthands for matrix operations in both spin-space, as well as sublattice space. The effective interaction responsible for the RPA scale as 𝒥i​j∼(1−αi​j)​Ji​j/αi​j​ti​j{\mathcal{J}}_{ij}\sim(1-\alpha_{ij})J_{ij}/\alpha_{ij}t_{ij} where ti​jt_{ij} is the self-consistent Dirac hopping generated |t1|≈0.2​J1​(1+Δ)|t_{1}|\approx 0.2J_{1}(1+\Delta) for small anisotropies. Lastly, since we want to compare with experimental results, we Fourier transform over actual real-space position, getting rid of the sublattice index, and obtain χa​b(𝐐,Ω)=∑i,jχi​ja​b(𝐐,Ω)e−i𝐐⋅(𝐫i−𝐫j)\chi_{ab}({{\bf{Q}}},\Omega)=\sum_{i,j}\chi_{ij}^{ab}({{\bf{Q}}},\Omega)e^{-i{{\bf{Q}}}\cdot(\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{r}_{j})}. The full dynamic spin structure factor at zero-temperature then is simply 𝐒(𝐐,Ω)=(1/π)(χx​x′′(𝐐,Ω)+χy​y′′(𝐐,Ω)+χz​z′′(𝐐,Ω))\mathbf{S}({{\bf{Q}}},\Omega)=(1/\pi)(\chi_{xx}^{{}^{\prime\prime}}({{\bf{Q}}},\Omega)+\chi_{yy}^{{}^{\prime\prime}}({{\bf{Q}}},\Omega)+\chi_{zz}^{{}^{\prime\prime}}({{\bf{Q}}},\Omega)).

Below, we compare the results of this approach with experimental data on a variety of recently studied triangular lattice antiferromagnets. The published experimental data are presented as false color plots of the scattering intensity to emphasize certain features; we have not aimed to reproduce the precise color scales, but instead we focus on highlighting that our approach captures several key features in the data as we discuss below.

IV.1 Heisenberg limit Δ=1\Delta=1

Fig.7 shows the real frequency dynamic spin structure factor 𝐒⁡(𝐐,Ω)\mathbf{S}({{\bf{Q}}},\Omega) for momenta along a high-symmetry path and all energies. Near the 𝚪1=(0,0)\bm{\Gamma}_{1}=(0,0) and 𝚪3=(2​π,2​3​π)\bm{\Gamma}_{3}=(2\pi,2\sqrt{3}\pi) points we find clear sharp weakly gapped modes, while at the 𝐊1=(2​π/3,2​π/3){{\bf{K}}}_{1}=(2\pi/3,2\pi/\sqrt{3}) and 𝐊2=(4​π/3,4​π/3){{\bf{K}}}_{2}=(4\pi/3,4\pi/\sqrt{3}) points, we find clear sharp gapless modes matching with magnon bands calculated from linear spin-wave theory around a coplanar order, with a continuum background coming from the spinons. Near the 𝐌2=(π,3​π){{\bf{M}}}_{2}=(\pi,\sqrt{3}\pi) and 𝐊1/2/2{{\bf{K}}}_{1/2}/2 points, we find a sharp soft mode which is approximately at half the energy of the expected lowest spin wave, along with a broad continuum coming from nesting of the Dirac nodes. The existence of a sharp mode coming down in energy at these momenta is in very good agreement with dynamics calculated through other methods like series expansion [68, 82, 83], magnon-magnon interaction effects [84, 85], VMC [47], and DMRG [86, 87]. Moreover, our results are in good qualitative agreement with INS experiments on Ba3CoSb2O9 [48, 50, 51, 49] which has been reported to have a small easy-plane anisotropy of Δ≈0.95\Delta\approx 0.95, and with KYbSe2 which is modeled by a Heisenberg spin model with J2/J1≈0.05J_{2}/J_{1}\approx 0.05 [58].

The advantages of our method are twofold. Firstly, not only do we capture the existence of these sharp magnon bands coming from linear spin wave theory, but also the continuum of spectrum expected from fractionalized excitations. The broad response at low energies e.g. around the 𝐌{{\bf{M}}} points is natural in the spinon language as coming from nesting of the Dirac nodes, a feature which even magnon-magnon interactions are not able to capture. Secondly, our approach is numerically much less intensive than calculating dynamics in many-body techniques like VMC and DMRG.

IV.2 Easy-axis anisotropy Δ>1\Delta>1

In this section, we again calculate the mean-field+RPA spin response but now in the presence of an anisotropy Δ>1\Delta>1. We plot the imaginary part of the in-plane susceptibility at a small anisotropy of Δ=1.8\Delta=1.8 relevant for Na2BaCo(PO4)2 in Fig.8. We again find clear sharp modes matching with magnon bands calculated from linear spin-wave theory around a supersolid order near the 𝚪\bm{\Gamma} and 𝐊{{\bf{K}}} points. The anisotropy pushes one of the spin-waves higher in energy ∝Δ\propto\Delta which is also seen in our RPA plot, with a strong continuum between the low-energy and high-energy modes. There still exists a soft sharp mode at the 𝐌{{\bf{M}}} and 𝐊/2{{\bf{K}}}/2 which is lower in energy than expected from spin-waves, along with a gapped continuum coming from the Dirac nodes nesting. This is again in good qualitative agreement with experimental results observed for Na2BaCo(PO4)2 [52, 53, 54] where similar features have been reported.

We expect from simple spin-wave theory that increasing the anisotropy Δ\Delta just pushes up the high-energy spin wave which is out-of-plane and hence its energy scales with Δ\Delta. We confirm this in our mean-field+RPA approach by repeating the analysis in a large Δ=10\Delta=10 regime which is relevant for materials like K2Co(SeO3)2 [55, 56] and Rb2Co(SeO3)2 [57] as plotted in Fig.9. We also plot the susceptibility over the entire Brillouin zone at a fixed low energy of Ω/t=1\Omega/t=1 in Fig.10 which we expect should be fairly independent of the anisotropy. We find this also to be in good qualitative agreement with experiments on K2Co(SeO3)2 [55, 56].

V Discussion

In this paper, we have shown that a modified extension of the usual large-NN S​U​(2​N)SU(2N) formalism for partons to a distinct S​U​(2​N)×S​U​(M)SU(2N)\times SU(M) version, which incorporates an additional ‘spin’ length κ=M/2​N\kappa=M/2N, is useful in treating gapless spin liquids and magnetically ordered phases democratically while suppressing gauge fluctuations. We have determined the phase diagram for the antiferromagnetic J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} Heisenberg model on the triangular lattice in the large-(N,M)(N,M) limit. The ground state phase diagram and order parameters from the mean field theory match with previously known numerical results for κ≈0.36\kappa\!\approx\!0.36. We phenomenologically adapt this approach to the J1−J2J_{1}\!-\!J_{2} XXZ model on the triangular lattice which includes easy-axis anisotropy. In this approach, we split the spin Hamiltonian (written in terms of fermionic partons) into two parts phenomenologically and decompose each using different HS fields: local dynamical Weiss fields, as well as spinon hopping fields assumed to be condensed around their mean-field value. We supplement the mean-field results with Gutzwiller projected wavefunctions studied using VMC where we find the phase diagram of the XXZ model as we tune J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1} and find good qualitative agreement with recent DMRG result [44, 45]. For small J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1}, we find that the ground state is a DSL with weak supersolid ordering which gaps the Dirac nodes and is thus expected to be a conventional ordered phase. With increasing J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1}, this supersolid gives way to a pure DSL at intermediate frustration. Finally, for larger J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1}, the DSL develops additional weak stripe order which again gaps out the Dirac nodes.

Next we turn to the dynamics of the spin model where we calculate dynamic spin susceptibility beyond mean-field level by including RPA corrections coming from fluctuations of the internal Weiss fields. This is justified for N,M≫1N,M\!\gg\!1 since RPA corrections are the leading order corrections to spin-correlations, as compared to gauge fluctuations which are sub-leading. We find the spin-susceptibility in the Heisenberg limit matches extremely well with previous many-body dynamics from VMC[47], DMRG [86, 87], and analytical results from series expansion [68, 82] and magnon-magnon interactions [84, 85]. Lastly, motivated by the Heisenberg limit, we calculate the dynamics for the anisotropic XXZ model and find very good agreement with INS experimental observations on materials like Ba3CoSb2O9 [48, 50, 51, 49], Na2BaCo(PO4)2  [52, 53, 54], K2Co(SeO3)2  [55, 56], and Rb2Co(SeO3)2 .

For future directions, it would be interesting to develop a diagrammatic route to our methodology which can be extended to include parton interaction diagrams beyond RPA and gauge fluctuation corrections, both of which might perhaps lead to improved quantitative agreement with experimental results. There exists a family of diagrams coming from corrections to the parton propagator which affects the dynamics at leading order compared to gauge fluctuations. However treating those will involve solving self-consistent Dyson equations and we leave that for a future work. Furthermore, it would be useful if a more formal extension can be derived for anisotropic Hamiltonians just like the S​U​(2)SU(2) symmetric Heisenberg Hamiltonians. We note that this is a general problem faced even in the usual S​U​(2​N)SU(2N) and S​p​(2​N)Sp(2N) formalisms and is an open question.

It would also be interesting to study and connect our current results to the low energy theory for the DSL which would consist of Nf=4N_{f}=4 flavour fermions coupled to a U⁡(1)U(1) gauge theory [33, 34]. Specifically, our approach treats the DSL to ordering transition as being induced by residual four-fermion interactions which have the same form as the original spin Hamiltonian. One needs to understand, however, the role that monopoles play in these possibly weakly ordered Dirac spin-liquids, and how they compete with four-fermion interaction induced symmetry breaking [36, 37]. Lastly, previous S​p​(2​N)Sp(2N) models have been utilized in doped regimes to understand charge orderings and superconductivity [22]. It would be of interest to understand if the same can be done in our S​U​(2​N)×S​U​(M)SU(2N)\times SU(M) model as well.

Regarding prospective materials where this approach is relevant, there is an abundance of candidates which order at T≪θC​WT\ll\theta_{CW}, but exhibit dynamics which are not completely characterized by simple LSWT. There has been a series of work on triangular lattice antiferromagnet YbMgGaO4 where a similar RPA enhanced mean-field spinon fermi surface state has been successful in describing inelastic neutron scattering experiments [88, 89, 90]. Further, recently, there has been a surge in DSL candidate materials on the triangular lattice such as YbZn2GaO5[91], and CeMgAl11O19 [92]. The INS spectra of YbZn2GaO5 appears to have a very flat continuum like response which does not naively seem compatible with a simple π\pi-flux state on the triangular lattice. Although DMRG recreates some features of the spectra, the underlying microscopic picture is not very clear. It would hence be interesting to understand the claims about DSL in these materials using our approach as well. Investigating these theoretical extensions and candidate materials would improve our understanding of the interplay between spinons, magnons, and gauge fluctuations in the dynamics of frustrated quantum magnets.

Appendix A S​U​(2​N)×S​U​(M)SU(2N)\times SU(M) Partons

We start with the usual S​U​(2)SU(2) fermionic partons where a local Spin operator SiaS_{i}^{a} is written in terms of fermions as

Sia=12​fi,α†​σα​βa​fi,β,fi,α†​fi,α=1​∀i,S_{i}^{a}=\frac{1}{2}f^{\dagger}_{i,\alpha}\sigma^{a}_{\alpha\beta}f_{i,\beta}\,,\>\>\>f^{\dagger}_{i,\alpha}f_{i,\alpha}=1\forall i\,, (11)

where ii represents a lattice site, α,β\alpha,\beta are S​U​(2)SU(2) indices in the fundamental representation with S​U​(2)SU(2) generators Ta=σa/2T^{a}=\sigma^{a}/2 for a∈{1,2,3}a\in\{1,2,3\}. A generic spin-spin S​U​(2)SU(2) invariant Hamiltonian has the form

ℋi​j=Ji​j​Sia⋅Sja=Ji​j​{12​fi,α†​fi,β​fj,β†​fj,α−14​fi,α†​fi,α​fj,β†​fj,β},\begin{split}{\mathcal{H}}_{ij}&=J_{ij}S_{i}^{a}\cdot S_{j}^{a}\\ &=J_{ij}\left\{\frac{1}{2}f^{\dagger}_{i,\alpha}f_{i,\beta}f^{\dagger}_{j,\beta}f_{j,\alpha}-\frac{1}{4}f^{\dagger}_{i,\alpha}f_{i,\alpha}f^{\dagger}_{j,\beta}f_{j,\beta}\right\}\,,\end{split} (12)

where we have used the completeness relation for S​U​(2)SU(2) generators in the second line. Note that the second quartic fermion term is just a constant since the fillings of the partons are set to 1 exactly (at the operator level itself).

We then enlarge the internal symmetry group to S​U​(2​N)SU(2N) introduce a dummy S​U​(M)SU(M) index on the partons fi,α,ℓf_{i,\alpha,\ell} where ii marks a lattice site, α∈{1,2,…,2​N}\alpha\in\{1,2,...,2N\}, and ℓ∈{1,2,…,M}\ell\in\{1,2,...,M\}. The Hamiltonian in Eq.(4) is a possible and natural extension of the usual S​U​(2)SU(2) Heisenberg Hamiltonian which is invariant under S​U​(2​N)×S​U​(M)SU(2N)\times SU(M). Now the fermion number constraint is still that of half-filling. Hence we have a single U⁡(1)U(1) gauge field coupled to 2​N​M≫12NM\gg 1 flavors of fermions and therefore gauge fluctuations are obviously suppressed. Furthermore, we have already argued in the main text why at the mean-field level such a Hamiltonian favors both hopping and on-site ordering for the partons, depending on the ratio of two large numbers κ⁡(N,M)≡M/2​N\kappa(N,M)\equiv M/2N. This ratio will turn out to play the role of the spin-length, consistent with the interpretation that a larger spin-length favors magnetic ordering and vice-versa. This interpretation can be formalized by looking at spin-sum rules.

Since there are infinitely many operators symmetric under S​U​(2​N)×S​U​(M)SU(2N)\times SU(M) which reduce to the usual spin-1/21/2 S​U​(2)SU(2) operators in the N=1,M=1N=1,M=1 case, we have a unique and weird freedom on our hands. We can choose the Hamiltonian to have a different form (based on what states we want to be competitive) than the spin-spin correlations in the structure factor, with the constraint that they match in the case of spin-1/21/2. There are some further restrictions that we should sensibly impose on a structure factor operator Oi​j​(N,M)O_{ij}(N,M) :

  • •

    Oi​j​(N=1,M=1)=Sia⋅SjaO_{ij}(N=1,M=1)=S_{i}^{a}\cdot S_{j}^{a} : The operator should reduce to the spin-1/21/2 spin-spin Heisenberg correlation exactly for N=M=1N=M=1.

  • •

    Oi​i​(N,M)=κ⁡(κ+1)O_{ii}(N,M)=\kappa(\kappa+1) for some κ⁡(N,M)∼𝒪⁡(1)\kappa(N,M)\sim{\mathcal{O}}(1) : The operator should reproduce the usual spin-sum rules irrespective of N,MN,M. Furthermore, κ⁡(N=1,M=1)=1/2\kappa(N=1,M=1)=1/2.

  • •

    (Optional) The operator should have contributions from both the disordered phase and ordered phase at the same order in (N,M)(N,M).

Lets look at the sum rule and try to understand how we can get an operator like that. We get a hint from the ordered state energy ∝M2​𝐦𝐢⋅𝐦𝐣\propto M^{2}\mathbf{m_{i}}\cdot\mathbf{m_{j}}. Intuitively, tuning NN favors the spin liquid and tuning MM favors the ordered state. Hence as mentioned earlier, κ=M/2​N\kappa=M/2N is roughly playing the role of the spin-length. With a little bit of trial and error we can come up with an operator which looks like

Oi​j=1N3​{12​fi,α,ℓ†​fi,β,ℓ​fj,β,ℓ′†​fj,α,ℓ′+12​fi,α,ℓ†​fi,α,ℓ′​fj,β,ℓ′†​fj,β,ℓ−14​N​(1+1κ)​fi,α,ℓ†​fi,α,ℓ​fj,β,ℓ′†​fj,β,ℓ′}.O_{ij}=\frac{1}{N^{3}}\left\{\frac{1}{2}f^{\dagger}_{i,\alpha,\ell}f_{i,\beta,\ell}f^{\dagger}_{j,\beta,\ell^{\prime}}f_{j,\alpha,\ell^{\prime}}+\frac{1}{2}f^{\dagger}_{i,\alpha,\ell}f_{i,\alpha,\ell^{\prime}}f^{\dagger}_{j,\beta,\ell^{\prime}}f_{j,\beta,\ell}-\frac{1}{4N}\left(1+\frac{1}{\kappa}\right)f^{\dagger}_{i,\alpha,\ell}f_{i,\alpha,\ell}f^{\dagger}_{j,\beta,\ell^{\prime}}f_{j,\beta,\ell^{\prime}}\right\}\,. (13)

Since the fermion filling is always fixed at half-filling exactly, we have that fi,α,ℓ†​fi,α,ℓ=N​M=2​N2​κf^{\dagger}_{i,\alpha,\ell}f_{i,\alpha,\ell}=NM=2N^{2}\kappa as an operator identity. Hence the operator in Eq.(13) can be simplified to

𝐒i⋅𝐒j→N,M≫1Oi​j=1N3​{12​fi,α,ℓ†​fi,β,ℓ​fj,β,ℓ′†​fj,α,ℓ′+12​fi,α,ℓ†​fi,α,ℓ′​fj,β,ℓ′†​fj,β,ℓ}−κ⁡(κ+1).\mathbf{S}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{j}\xrightarrow{N,M\gg 1}O_{ij}=\frac{1}{N^{3}}\left\{\frac{1}{2}f^{\dagger}_{i,\alpha,\ell}f_{i,\beta,\ell}f^{\dagger}_{j,\beta,\ell^{\prime}}f_{j,\alpha,\ell^{\prime}}+\frac{1}{2}f^{\dagger}_{i,\alpha,\ell}f_{i,\alpha,\ell^{\prime}}f^{\dagger}_{j,\beta,\ell^{\prime}}f_{j,\beta,\ell}\right\}-\kappa(\kappa+1)\,. (14)

Let us now carefully analyze why this operator satisfies all of the aforementioned requirements. Some properties of these operators that will prove useful are as follows

  • •

    On-site sum rules for the operators in Eq.(14) cannot be found individually without additional operator constraints on the partons. However, we can relate the two as follows

    fi,α,ℓ†​fi,α,ℓ′​fi,β,ℓ′†​fi,β,ℓ=fi,α,ℓ†​fi,α,ℓ′​(δℓ,ℓ′​δβ​β−fi,β,ℓ​fi,β,ℓ′†)=2​N2​M+fi,α,ℓ†​fi,β,ℓ​fi,α,ℓ′​fi,β,ℓ′†=2​N2​M+fi,α,ℓ†​fi,β,ℓ​(δℓ′,ℓ′​δα​β−fi,β,ℓ′†​fi,α,ℓ′)=2​N2​M+N​M2−fi,α,ℓ†​fi,β,ℓ​fj,β,ℓ′†​fj,α,ℓ′.\begin{split}f^{\dagger}_{i,\alpha,\ell}f_{i,\alpha,\ell^{\prime}}f^{\dagger}_{i,\beta,\ell^{\prime}}f_{i,\beta,\ell}&=f^{\dagger}_{i,\alpha,\ell}f_{i,\alpha,\ell^{\prime}}\left(\delta_{\ell,\ell^{\prime}}\delta_{\beta\beta}-f_{i,\beta,\ell}f^{\dagger}_{i,\beta,\ell^{\prime}}\right)\\ &=2N^{2}M+f^{\dagger}_{i,\alpha,\ell}f_{i,\beta,\ell}f_{i,\alpha,\ell^{\prime}}f^{\dagger}_{i,\beta,\ell^{\prime}}\\ &=2N^{2}M+f^{\dagger}_{i,\alpha,\ell}f_{i,\beta,\ell}\left(\delta_{\ell^{\prime},\ell^{\prime}}\delta_{\alpha\beta}-f^{\dagger}_{i,\beta,\ell^{\prime}}f_{i,\alpha,\ell^{\prime}}\right)\\ &=2N^{2}M+NM^{2}-f^{\dagger}_{i,\alpha,\ell}f_{i,\beta,\ell}f^{\dagger}_{j,\beta,\ell^{\prime}}f_{j,\alpha,\ell^{\prime}}\,.\end{split} (15)

    Hence, Oi​i=(1/2​N3)​(2​N2​M+N​M2)−κ⁡(κ+1)=κ⁡(κ+1)O_{ii}=(1/2N^{3})(2N^{2}M+NM^{2})-\kappa(\kappa+1)=\kappa(\kappa+1) with κ⁡(N,M)=M/2​N\kappa(N,M)=M/2N which satisfies the sum rule condition s.t. κ⁡(N=1,M=1)=1/2\kappa(N=1,M=1)=1/2. Connecting with our α,1−α\alpha,1-\alpha decomposition, we find that α∼1/(1+2​κ)≈1/2​κ\alpha\sim 1/(1+2\kappa)\approx 1/2\kappa for large spin-length akin to a spin-wave expansion.

  • •

    For the case of N=1,M=1N=1,M=1, it turns out that fi,α,ℓ†​fi,α,ℓ′​fj,β,ℓ′†​fj,β,ℓ=1f^{\dagger}_{i,\alpha,\ell}f_{i,\alpha,\ell^{\prime}}f^{\dagger}_{j,\beta,\ell^{\prime}}f_{j,\beta,\ell}=1. Therefore, Oi​j→N=M=1(1/2)​fi,α,ℓ†​fi,β,ℓ​fj,β,ℓ′†​fj,α,ℓ′−(1/4)O_{ij}\xrightarrow{N=M=1}(1/2)f^{\dagger}_{i,\alpha,\ell}f_{i,\beta,\ell}f^{\dagger}_{j,\beta,\ell^{\prime}}f_{j,\alpha,\ell^{\prime}}-(1/4) which matches the usual S​U​(2)SU(2) spin-spin Heisenberg correlation.

Appendix B Path Integral

We first start with the usual S​U​(2)SU(2) symmetric Hamiltonian

ℋ=12​∑i,jJi​j​fi,α†​fi,β​fj,β†​fj,α{\mathcal{H}}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i,j}J_{ij}f^{\dagger}_{i,\alpha}f_{i,\beta}f^{\dagger}_{j,\beta}f_{j,\alpha} (16)

such that the total action looks like (replacing f†f^{\dagger} with f¯\bar{f} in the path integral)

𝒮[f¯,f,a0]=∫dτ(∑if¯i,α(∂τ−ai0)fi,α+ℋ(τ)).{\mathcal{S}}[\bar{f},f,a_{0}]=\int d\tau\left(\sum_{i}\bar{f}_{i,\alpha}(\partial_{\tau}-a_{i}^{0})f_{i,\alpha}+{\mathcal{H}}(\tau)\right)\,. (17)

Now, we are going to decompose the four fermion interaction in the Hamiltonian democratically in the ordered and disordered channel, akin to usual Hartree-Fock. In the disordered channel we need Hubbard-Stratonovich fields which live on the bonds, wi​j​(τ)w_{ij}(\tau), the condensate of which give rise to parton hoppings at the mean-field level. Now, there are two kinds of fluctuations of wi​j=|wi​j|​e−i​ai​jw_{ij}=|w_{ij}|e^{-ia_{ij}}. The strength modulation must be gapped [28], and hence can be safely ignored in the low energy physics. The only fluctuations to keep track of are the gauge fluctuations aμa_{\mu}. Now assuming that the mean-field disordered state is a Dirac state such as the π\pi-flux state, one can linearize the Hamiltonian and go to the continuum limit [33, 34]. In this limit, the low energy theory looks like QED-3 with Nf=4N_{f}=4 flavors of fermions

𝒮=∫d3x[ψ¯α(x)(i∂̸−a̸)ψα(x)+14​g2F2],{\mathcal{S}}=\int d^{3}x\>\left[\bar{\psi}_{\alpha}(x)(i\not{\partial}-\not{a})\psi_{\alpha}(x)+\frac{1}{4g^{2}}F^{2}\right]\,, (18)

where F2F^{2} is a Maxwell term generated by integrating out the high-energy fermion modes above some RG scale. Importantly, the Maxwell term is generated at leading order by a fermion bubble diagram, and hence is ∝Nf\propto N_{f}. Hence, in our extension of S​U​(2​N)×S​U​(M)SU(2N)\times SU(M), we will get the continuum action in the disordered phase as

𝒮=∫d3x[ψ¯α,ℓ(x)(i∂̸−a̸)ψα,ℓ(x)+2​N​M4​g2F2].{\mathcal{S}}=\int d^{3}x\>\left[\bar{\psi}_{\alpha,\ell}(x)(i\not{\partial}-\not{a})\psi_{\alpha,\ell}(x)+\frac{2NM}{4g^{2}}F^{2}\right]\,. (19)

Note that if we naively look at the scaling of the Hamiltonian in Eq.(19), it scales as 𝒪⁡(N​M){\mathcal{O}}(NM). Remember that in the N,M≫1N,M\gg 1 limit Hamiltonian, the disordered state had energy scaling as 𝒪⁡(N2​M){\mathcal{O}}(N^{2}M) and hence the action above is associated with a rescaled exchange 𝕁=J/N\mathbb{J}=J/N. We use this fact in the ordered channel to get

exp⁡(−1N​ℋi​j)=∫∏a=14​N2−1d​hia​d​hja​exp⁡(c1​hia​Ji​j−1​hja−c2​f¯i,α,ℓ​Tα​βa​fi,β,ℓ​hja−c2​hia​f¯j,α,ℓ​Tα​βa​fj,β,ℓ),c22c1=12​N,\exp\left(-\frac{1}{N}{\mathcal{H}}_{ij}\right)=\int\prod_{a=1}^{4N^{2}-1}dh_{i}^{a}dh_{j}^{a}\exp\left(c_{1}h_{i}^{a}J^{-1}_{ij}h_{j}^{a}-c_{2}\bar{f}_{i,\alpha,\ell}T^{a}_{\alpha\beta}f_{i,\beta,\ell}h_{j}^{a}-c_{2}h_{i}^{a}\bar{f}_{j,\alpha,\ell}T^{a}_{\alpha\beta}f_{j,\beta,\ell}\right)\,,\>\>\>\frac{c_{2}^{2}}{c_{1}}=\frac{1}{2N}\,, (20)

where hia​(τ)=∑⟨j⟩Ji​j​mjah_{i}^{a}(\tau)=\sum_{\expectationvalue{j}}J_{ij}m_{j}^{a} can be interpreted as the dynamic internal Weiss field generated on site ii. We have an overall freedom in choosing the coefficients c1c_{1} and c2c_{2} in Eq.(20), however again these can be fixed by simple scaling arguments. We want the expectation value of both of the terms in Eq.(20) to come from the ordered state part of (1/N)​ℋ(1/N){\mathcal{H}} and hence scale as 𝒪⁡(M2){\mathcal{O}}(M^{2}). With the interpretation of hiah_{i}^{a} as being NN copies of internal S​U​(2)SU(2) Weiss fields, we know already that ⟨hia​hja⟩∼𝒪⁡(N)\expectationvalue{h_i^a h_j^a}\sim{\mathcal{O}}(N) and hence we can fix c1=M2/2​Nc_{1}=M^{2}/2N and c2=M/2​Nc_{2}=M/2N. This is consistent since ⟨hia​f¯i,α,ℓ​Tα​βa​fi,β,ℓ⟩∼𝒪⁡(N​M)\expectationvalue{h_i^a \bar{f}_{i, \a, \ell}T^{a}_{\a\b}f_{i, \b, \ell}}\sim{\mathcal{O}}(NM). Therefore, combining everything, the full S​U​(2​N)×S​U​(M)SU(2N)\times SU(M) low energy theory will look like (switching to momentum space)

𝒮=∫d3​k​[ψ¯α,ℓ​(k)​k̸​ψα,ℓ​(k)+2​N​M4​g2​F2+M22​N​ha​(k)​𝒥−1​(k)​ha​(−k)]+∫d3​k​d3​q​[M2​N​ha​(q)​ψ¯α,ℓ​(k+q)​Tα​βa​ψβ,ℓ​(k)+ψ¯α,ℓ​(k+q)​a̸​(q)​ψα,ℓ​(k)],\begin{split}{\mathcal{S}}=&\int d^{3}k\>\left[\bar{\psi}_{\alpha,\ell}(k)\not{k}\psi_{\alpha,\ell}(k)+\frac{2NM}{4g^{2}}F^{2}+\frac{M^{2}}{2N}h^{a}(k){\mathcal{J}}^{-1}(k)h^{a}(-k)\right]\\ +&\int d^{3}k\>d^{3}q\>\left[\frac{M}{2N}h^{a}(q)\bar{\psi}_{\alpha,\ell}(k+q)T^{a}_{\alpha\beta}\psi_{\beta,\ell}(k)+\bar{\psi}_{\alpha,\ell}(k+q)\not{a}(q)\psi_{\alpha,\ell}(k)\right]\,,\end{split} (21)

where 𝒥⁡(𝐤){\mathcal{J}}({{\bf{k}}}) is the Weiss field propagator dependent on the exchange interactions on the lattice. We can rescale the gauge field aa and the Weiss field hh and rewrite the action as

𝒮=∫d3​k​[ψ¯α,ℓ​(k)​k̸​ψα,ℓ​(k)+14​F~2+h~a​(k)​𝒥−1​(k)​h~a​(−k)]+∫d3​k​d3​q​[12​N​h~a​(q)​ψ¯α,ℓ​(k+q)​Tα​βa​ψβ,ℓ​(k)+g2​N​M​ψ¯α,ℓ​(k+q)​a~​(q)​ψα,ℓ​(k)].\begin{split}{\mathcal{S}}=&\int d^{3}k\>\left[\bar{\psi}_{\alpha,\ell}(k)\not{k}\psi_{\alpha,\ell}(k)+\frac{1}{4}\tilde{F}^{2}+\tilde{h}^{a}(k){\mathcal{J}}^{-1}(k)\tilde{h}^{a}(-k)\right]\\ +&\int d^{3}k\>d^{3}q\>\left[\frac{1}{\sqrt{2N}}\tilde{h}^{a}(q)\bar{\psi}_{\alpha,\ell}(k+q)T^{a}_{\alpha\beta}\psi_{\beta,\ell}(k)+\frac{g}{\sqrt{2NM}}\bar{\psi}_{\alpha,\ell}(k+q)\not{\tilde{a}}(q)\psi_{\alpha,\ell}(k)\right]\,.\end{split} (22)

Therefore we find that the Nf=2​N​MN_{f}=2NM flavors of fermions at low energy are interacting with Nb=N2−1N_{b}=N^{2}-1 flavors of bosons h~a\tilde{h}^{a} with a coupling of gh=1/2​Ng_{h}=1/\sqrt{2N}, and with a U⁡(1)U(1) gauge field a~\tilde{a} with a coupling of ga=g/2​N​Mg_{a}=g/\sqrt{2NM}. The gauge coupling being ga∝gh/Mg_{a}\propto g_{h}/\sqrt{M} is what leads to the fact that leading order corrections to the spin-susceptibility come from RPA diagrams of the boson h~\tilde{h}, instead of gauge corrections to the fermion propagator and the vertex. Note that because of spin-sums, RPA gauge corrections to the spin susceptibility vanish to all orders.

Now, in the symmetry broken phase, the Weiss fields have a non-zero expectation value around which we can consider excitations h~a​(k)=h~0a​δ​(k)+δ​h~a​(k)\tilde{h}^{a}(k)=\tilde{h}_{0}^{a}\delta(k)+\delta\tilde{h}^{a}(k). The uniform condensate part will give the fermions a matrix mass as (1/N)​ψ¯α,ℓ​(k)​h~0a​Tα​βa​ψβ,ℓ​(k)(1/\sqrt{N})\bar{\psi}_{\alpha,\ell}(k)\tilde{h}_{0}^{a}T^{a}_{\alpha\beta}\psi_{\beta,\ell}(k). The full low-energy action in the ordered phase hence looks like (upto a total constant corresponding to the energy of the condensate)

𝒮=∫d3​k​[ψ¯α,ℓ​(k)​(k̸​δα​β−1N​h~0a​Tα​βa)​ψβ,ℓ​(k)+14​F~2+δ​h~a​(k)​𝒥−1​(k)​δ​h~a​(−k)]+∫d3​k​d3​q​[12​N​δ​h~a​(q)​ψ¯α,ℓ​(k+q)​Tα​βa​ψβ,ℓ​(k)+g2​N​M​ψ¯α,ℓ​(k+q)​a~​(q)​ψα,ℓ​(k)].\begin{split}{\mathcal{S}}=&\int d^{3}k\>\left[\bar{\psi}_{\alpha,\ell}(k)\left(\not{k}\delta_{\alpha\beta}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\tilde{h}_{0}^{a}T^{a}_{\alpha\beta}\right)\psi_{\beta,\ell}(k)+\frac{1}{4}\tilde{F}^{2}+\delta\tilde{h}^{a}(k){\mathcal{J}}^{-1}(k)\delta\tilde{h}^{a}(-k)\right]\\ +&\int d^{3}k\>d^{3}q\>\left[\frac{1}{\sqrt{2N}}\delta\tilde{h}^{a}(q)\bar{\psi}_{\alpha,\ell}(k+q)T^{a}_{\alpha\beta}\psi_{\beta,\ell}(k)+\frac{g}{\sqrt{2NM}}\bar{\psi}_{\alpha,\ell}(k+q)\not{\tilde{a}}(q)\psi_{\alpha,\ell}(k)\right]\,.\end{split} (23)

One can therefore integrate out the fermions altogether from this theory and get an effective action in terms of the Weiss field excitations δ​h~a\delta\tilde{h}^{a} and the gauge boson aμa_{\mu}. Note that since h~a\tilde{h}^{a} are not charged under aμa_{\mu} (they are gauge invariant fields) so are δ​h~a\delta\tilde{h}^{a}. Hence, integrating out the fermions cannot couple δ​h~a\delta\tilde{h}^{a} with aμa_{\mu} directly, it can only couple δ​h~a\delta\tilde{h}^{a} to gauge invariant operators like Fμ​νF_{\mu\nu} (e.g. ∂μδ​h~a​∂νδ​h~a​Fμ​ν\partial_{\mu}\delta\tilde{h}^{a}\partial_{\nu}\delta\tilde{h}^{a}F^{\mu\nu}). Therefore the effective action at leading order (quadratic) would entirely consist of decoupled sectors 𝒮e​f​f​[δ​h~]+𝒮e​f​f​[aμ]{\mathcal{S}}_{eff}[\delta\tilde{h}]+{\mathcal{S}}_{eff}[a_{\mu}]. Now we know that once the charged fermions are gapped in a compact U⁡(1)U(1) gauge theory in 2+12+1 dimensions, monopoles are allowed to proliferate [94]. Monopoles in our formulation correspond to 2​π2\pi local flux insertions of aμa_{\mu} in Eq.(21). Subsequently, the photons are gapped and there are no residual gapless gauge excitations. The effective low energy action is simply that of the Weiss fields themselves 𝒮e​f​f​[δ​h~]{\mathcal{S}}_{eff}[\delta\tilde{h}], just like a conventional magnet. To leading order, it will schematically be

𝒮e​f​f​[δ​h~]=∫d3​k​[δ​h~a​(k)​(δa​b​𝒥−1​(k)−MN​χ0a​b​(k))​δ​h~b​(−k)]+𝒪⁡(δ​h~4),\begin{split}{\mathcal{S}}_{eff}[\delta\tilde{h}]=&\int d^{3}k\>\left[\delta\tilde{h}^{a}(k)\left(\delta^{ab}{\mathcal{J}}^{-1}(k)-\frac{M}{N}\chi_{0}^{ab}(k)\right)\delta\tilde{h}^{b}(-k)\right]+{\mathcal{O}}(\delta\tilde{h}^{4})\,,\end{split} (24)

where χ0a​b​(k)\chi_{0}^{ab}(k) is the mean-field spin susceptibility coming from the fermion bubble diagram per flavor ℓ\ell in S​U​(M)SU(M).

Appendix C VMC

In our VMC implementation, the auxillary parton Hamiltonian we have considered looks like

ℋf=−∑⟨i,j⟩1ti​j(f†i,αfj,α+h.c.)−12∑ihiaf†i,ασaα​βfi,β,\begin{split}{\mathcal{H}}^{f}=-\sum_{\expectationvalue{i, j}_{1}}t_{ij}\left(f^{\dagger}_{i,\alpha}f_{j,\alpha}+\mathrm{h.c.}\right)-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i}h_{i}^{a}f^{\dagger}_{i,\alpha}\sigma^{a}_{\alpha\beta}f_{i,\beta}\,,\end{split} (25)

where |ti​j|=1|t_{ij}|=1 can be held fixed. The site-dependent Weiss fields hiah_{i}^{a} depend on the specific ordering pattern being considered. In this paper we worked with a L=4×4×6L=4\times 4\times 6 triangular lattice with an enlarged unit cell of 66 sites to accommodate (a) 𝐐=𝐊{{\bf{Q}}}={{\bf{K}}} ordering like the 120∘120^{\circ} coplanar, or the supersolid ordering, (b) 𝐐=𝐌{{\bf{Q}}}={{\bf{M}}} ordering like the stripe order, and (c) a π\pi-flux state. The co-planar and collinear orders can be captured by a single Weiss field strength hh whereas the supersolid order requires three independent Weiss fields to keep track of.

The mean-field ground state |ψMFT⟩\ket{\psi_{\mathrm{MFT}}} can then be found by diagonalizing this quadratic Hamiltonian and filling states upto half-filling. This mean-field state variational state is then Gutzwiller projected to get the full many-body spin wavefunction |ψ⟩=|ψ⁡({t3,hi,gi​j})⟩=exp(−∑i,jgi​jS^izS^jz)P^|ψMFT​(t3,hi)⟩\ket{\psi}=\ket{\psi(\{t_3, h_i, g_{ij}\})}=\exp\left(-\sum_{i,j}g_{ij}\hat{S}_{i}^{z}\hat{S}_{j}^{z}\right)\hat{P}\ket{\psi_{\mathrm{MFT}}(t_3, h_i)}, where gi​jg_{ij} are long-range (upto 10t​h10^{th} nearest-neighbor) Jastrow factors to further enhance spin-correlations. We then measure the expectation value of the full spin Hamiltonian in Eq.(8) as E⁡({hi,gi​j})=⟨ψ​|ℋ𝒮|​ψ⟩/⟨ψ|ψ⟩E(\{h_{i},g_{ij}\})=\expectationvalue{\psi| \mh^{\ms} |\psi}/\expectationvalue{\psi|\psi} by sampling the many-body wavefunction through 10,000 (thermalization) + 10,000 (measurement) Monte Carlo sweeps. This energy is then optimized w.r.t the variational parameters of the wavefunction using stochastic reconfiguration gradient descent [61] for 250 steps. The optimized Jastrow factors in the supersolid ordered phase are plotted in Fig.11

Appendix D Mean-field DSL properties

Here we mention a few details about the mean-field state for the DSL and supersolid phase. The DSL is realized through the so called π\pi-flux state where each spin of the parton sees a gauge flux of 00 or π\pi in the up and down triangles of the lattice. This state as shown in Fig.12 does not break any physical symmetries (the π\pi and 00 flux can be interchanged through a particle-hole transformation on the partons) like translation or rotation. However, the parton hoppings naively seem to break some symmetries in a fixed gauge choice and requires doubling the unit cell to two sublattices. The resulting Dirac nodes shown in Fig.13 in the band structure are related by inversion, and doubly degenerate due to spin-↑\uparrow and spin-↓\downarrow.

To accommodate the supersolid order and stripe order on top of the DSL, one needs to enlarge the unit cell further to hold 6 sublattices. The supersolid order gaps out the Dirac nodes through its in-plane component, while also splits spin-degeneracy because of its out-of-plane component. The stripe order also gaps out the Dirac nodes. The band structures and corresponding density of states are shown in Fig.13 and Fig.14.
